title: Debt Reduction Strategies & Emergency Fund Sizing Playbook
publisher: Financial Planning Standards Board & Consumer Finance Education
summary: Standardized mathematical playbooks for debt acceleration (Avalanche vs Snowball), handling unexpected income drops or medical shocks, and adaptive replanning rules.

chunks.title: Debt Avalanche vs. Debt Snowball Methodology
chunks.text: When resolving multiple debt obligations, the Debt Avalanche method is mathematically optimal: all surplus cash is focused on the debt carrying the highest interest rate (e.g. credit card revolving balances at 42% APR or personal loans at 16% APR) while paying minimum dues on lower-rate debts (e.g. home loans at 8.5% APR). The Debt Snowball method focuses on the smallest balance first for psychological momentum. In both approaches, discretionary expenditures should be trimmed by 30% to 50% during the debt acceleration period.

chunks.title: Adaptive Replanning Triggers During Financial Shocks
chunks.text: When an individual experiences an unexpected financial shock—such as a >10% salary reduction, unexpected medical emergency bill, or substantial inflation in rent—the financial plan must adapt immediately: (1) Temporarily suspend discretionary milestone goals, (2) Redirect all non-essential budget surpluses to replenish the depleted emergency fund back to 3 months of baseline expenses, (3) Extend long-term goal timelines rather than liquidating provident fund or retirement assets.

chunks.title: Prudent Large Purchase Affordability Test
chunks.text: Before committing to a discretionary large one-time purchase (e.g. high-end laptop, luxury appliance, vehicle down payment), verify the 3-Step Affordability Rule: (1) The purchase must not reduce liquid emergency reserves below the 3-month survival floor, (2) The user must not rely on short-term high-interest credit or zero-downpayment balloon financing, (3) The resulting goal delay on higher-priority commitments must be under 3 months.
